entries.description:
The Syntax Helper exposes every language keyword, built-in function, primitive type, and metadata accessor available inside an OES configuration. It is read-only documentation that lives alongside the editor — it never modifies your configuration on its own.

Three tabs cover three navigation patterns. Contents groups entries by category. Index lists every name alphabetically with prefix-search. Search runs a token query across names + signatures.

Use the toolbar Back / Forward buttons to retrace your steps, Reload to pull in newly added help files without restarting, Sync to look up the identifier under the editor caret, and the Larger / Smaller text buttons to scale the description font. Press RawCtrl+F1 (Ctrl+F1 on Windows / Linux) in the editor to open the helper on the identifier under the cursor; RawCtrl+Alt+F1 toggles the pane.

Drag-and-drop: pick an entry in the Index or Search list (or the Contents tree) and drag it into the editor — the matching syntax template inserts at the drop position. The template respects the active compile mode (CES braces vs VES End* terminators).

entries.signature: from <item> in <source> [where ...] [orderby K1[, K2...] [ascending|descending]] [group ... by ... [into ...]] select ...
entries.description:
LINQ — language-integrated queries against in-memory collections. Two parallel surfaces compile to the same primitives.

**Block syntax** (eager): `from <var> in <source>` opens the query; `where / var / orderby K1[, K2...] [asc|desc] / group X by K [into g] / join b in Y on a.K equals b.K / skip N / take N / distinct` clauses; closes with `select <expr>` or `select { F = expr, ... }`. Materialises to an Array immediately.

**Chain syntax** (lazy): `arr.Where(λ).Select(λ).Distinct().Take(10).ToArray()`. 31 operations available — pipeline (Where / Select / Distinct / OrderBy / OrderByDescending / GroupBy / Join / Skip / Take / SkipWhile / TakeWhile / Reverse / Concat / Union / Intersect / Except / WhereIndexed / SelectIndexed), terminals (Count / ToArray / First / Last / Single / Any / ElementAt / Contains / SequenceEqual / Aggregate plus *OrDefault variants), aggregations (Sum / Min / Max / Average — with optional lambda selector).

Lambdas close over outer-scope locals: `var k = 5; arr.Where(Function(x) { return x > k; })`.

LINQ keywords compile identically in CES and VES modes.
entries.syntax_block:
var q = from o in orders
        where o.Total > 100
        var doubled = o.Total * 2
        orderby o.Warehouse, o.Date descending
        select { N = o.N, V = doubled };
entries.return_descr: Array of selected rows (block syntax) or lazy iterable (chain syntax).

entries.description:
A FUNCTION CAN BE A VALUE. `Function(x) { return x * 2; }` written where a value is expected produces a callable that can be stored, passed, returned and called later. Same keyword as a declaration; what makes it a value is the position it stands in.

WHAT THEY ARE FOR — three jobs, and finding yourself in one of them is how to know a lambda is wanted:

1. A CALLBACK — work handed to somebody else to run: `arr.Where(Function(x) { return x > k; })`. The collection decides WHEN to call it and with what; you only say what to do with one element.

2. AN EVENT HANDLER — behaviour attached to something that will happen later, without declaring a named procedure for it.

3. A RULE PASSED AS AN ARGUMENT — a comparison, a filter, a projection given to a routine that would otherwise be fixed: `Function Apply(f, v) { return f(v); }`.

THEY REMEMBER WHERE THEY WERE WRITTEN (closure). A lambda reads the locals around it — of the procedure and of the module — and reads them AT CALL TIME, not when it was written:

    var n = 1;
    var f = Function(x) { return x + n; };
    n = 100;
    f(0)   // 100

A parameter of the same name shadows the captured one, and the outer value is left untouched.

CALLING ONE THAT LIVES IN A CONTAINER GOES THROUGH A VARIABLE: `s.f(1)` and `a[0](1)` do not compile, while `var g = s.f; g(1)` does.

⚠ DO NOT REACH FOR A LAMBDA WHERE A CLAUSE SAYS IT SHORTER. Filtering, projecting, sorting and grouping a collection are written with KEYWORDS, and every lambda those would need is text you do not have to write:

    from x in arr where x > limit select x                      // short
    arr.Where(Function(x) { return x > limit; }).ToArray()      // the same thing, twice as long

Keep lambdas for the three jobs above — a callback, a handler, a rule handed to somebody else. See guide.linq for the clause order.
